cards.front: Define the quality factor Q of an oscillator in terms of stored energy.
cards.back: Q = 2π × (energy stored / energy dissipated per oscillation cycle). Equivalently, Q = ω₀ × (energy stored / average power loss).

cards.front: What does a high Q value physically indicate about damping and resonance?
cards.back: High Q means low damping (narrow resonance peak), long-lived oscillations, and sharp frequency selectivity.

cards.front: Give the relation between Q, resonant frequency ω₀ and full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) bandwidth Δω.
cards.back: Q = ω₀ / Δω (or Q = f₀ / Δf). This follows from the Lorentzian shape of the power resonance curve.

cards.front: For a damped harmonic oscillator ẍ + 2βẋ + ω₀²x = 0, express Q in terms of ω₀ and β.
cards.back: Q = ω₀ / (2β). β is the damping constant; underdamped solutions require β < ω₀.

cards.front: Relate Q to the amplitude decay time constant τ (time for amplitude to fall by 1/e).
cards.back: Q = ω₀ τ / 2. Energy decays twice as fast, with time constant τ/2.

cards.front: Derive Q from the ratio of stored energy E to power dissipated at resonance for a driven oscillator.
cards.back: At steady state, average power input = β m ω₀² A². Stored energy E = ½ m ω₀² A². Thus Q = ω₀ E / P_avg = ω₀/(2β).

cards.front: What is Q for a critically damped oscillator? Why is this value the boundary?
cards.back: Q = ½. At Q = ½, β = ω₀ so roots are real and repeated; any lower Q yields overdamped non-oscillatory decay.
